talk.title: Whose is it?
talk.task: Lost-and-found role-play: “Is this your phone?” “No, mine has a blue case.”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Role-play a lost-and-found office. Hold up one object at a time and ask 'Is this your ...?' or 'Does this belong to your friend?'. I answer with possessive pronouns and adjectives (No, mine is black. / I think it's hers. / Their umbrella is bigger.). Check my use of my/mine, your/yours, her/hers, our/ours, their/theirs and its/it's.

lines: Which pronoun? You don't know if it's he or she.

lines: Plural nouns take they / their. Problem solved.

items.title: everyone, somebody, no one…
lines: They take a singular verb.

items.title: Formal or everyday?

examples.text: Somebody left his book on the desk.
Everyone has his or her own ideas.

Everyone has their own ideas.

items.tip: In conversation, their is normal. In formal writing, use his or her, or a plural noun.

items.text: One classmate to another: Look. Somebody left ___ book on my desk.

lines: A student… his or her (formal). Easier: Students… their.
everyone / somebody + singular verb. Everyday speech: their.

examples.text: Students need to complete their assignments on time.
Everyone has their own ideas.

items.text: You are writing an article about seat belts. Which sentence is the smoothest?
options: A driver needs to put on his or her seat belt as soon as he or she gets in his or her car.
Drivers need to put on their seat belts as soon as they get in their cars.
items.why: Plural avoids “his or her” again and again.

items.text: When a student wants to study, he or she should find a quiet place.
options: When students want to study, they should find a quiet place.
When students wants to study, he should find a quiet place.

All students has to spend three hours in the laboratory, where they does experiments with his lab partners.

levels.title: The team: it or they?

lesson.title: Learn: it or they for groups

items.title: One unit, or people?

examples.text: My family is large. It is composed of nine members.
My family is loving. They are always ready to help me. I love them very much.

items.tip: Size, numbers, rules → it. Feelings and actions of people → they.

items.title: Group words
lines: family, team, class, jury, crowd, committee, faculty.
chips: The crowd was huge. It exceeded 100,000 people.
The crowd got excited. They began to shout.

items.text: A basketball team is small. ___ doesn't have many members.

items.title: Sometimes both are fine
lines: It's a matter of how you see the group.
chips: The committee meets once a month. It doesn't have much business.

lines: The group as one unit → it. The people in the group → they / them.
Sometimes both are possible.

examples.text: My family is large. It is composed of nine members.
My family is loving. They are always ready to help me.

items.text: I have a wonderful family. I love THEM very much.

items.text: The crowd at the soccer game was huge. IT exceeded 100,000 people.
items.why: The size of the unit → it.

items.text: The crowd became excited. THEY began to shout and wave flags.

A basketball team is relatively small. IT doesn't have many members.

items.text: The faculty wants a bigger lunch room. ___ around one small table.
The faculty has a weekly meeting. ___ ongoing changes to the curriculum.
items.why: The faculty as one unit → It makes.

talk.title: Selfies: your opinion
talk.task: Is it healthy to take lots of pictures of yourself? Tell Claude what you think.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Give me one statement at a time about selfies and ask if I agree: 'People who take a lot of pictures of themselves like themselves too much.' / 'It's healthy to like yourself.' / 'If you need to take a lot of pictures of yourself, you need a lot of attention.' I answer with my opinion using reflexive pronouns (myself, yourself, themselves, ourselves). Check that the reflexive pronoun matches the subject.

talk.title: Power stances
talk.task: How do people in your culture show they feel strong or confident? Tell Claude.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Amy Cuddy says that high-power stances (arms up, leaning back) help people feel confident about themselves. Ask me one question at a time: Are these power stances acceptable in your culture? What do people in your culture do to show power? How do you make yourself feel confident before an exam or interview? Check my reflexive pronouns.

levels.title: You = anyone
levels.full: Using You, One, and They as Impersonal Pronouns

items.title: you can mean everybody
lines: You should always be polite. = People should always be polite.
chips: How do you get to Fifth Avenue? (everyday)
How does one get to Fifth Avenue? (very formal)

items.title: one vs. you

examples.text: One should always be polite.
One gets what one pays for.
You should always be polite.
You get what you pay for.

items.tip: In academic writing, don't use “you” for people in general.

items.title: they = some people out there
lines: They = people in a place or company. We don't say who.
chips: Iowa is an agricultural state. They grow a lot of corn there. (they = farmers)
They never give you enough room on airplanes. (they = airlines)

items.text: Wool requires special care. If you wash wool in hot water, it will shrink. Who is “you”?
items.why: It's true for anybody who washes wool.

items.title: we for rules
lines: Parents use we to teach children rules.
chips: Tommy, we do not chew with our mouths open.

items.text: Alex, I told you not to wash your sweater in hot water! Who is “you”?
items.why: The speaker is talking to Alex.

lines: you / one = anyone, people in general. one is formal.
they = people out there (farmers, airlines, the government).

examples.text: You get what you pay for.
They grow a lot of corn in Iowa.

items.text: Kyung quit his job and went to art school. I think you need to follow your dreams.

items.why: The speaker is talking to Jake.

Sonya, let's make a deal. If you wash the clothes, I'll fold them.
items.why: The speaker is talking to Sonya.

If the person in front of you puts his seat back, you can barely move.
“You can't teach an old dog new tricks.”
options: It's hard for people to change old habits.
items.why: you = anyone. The dog = a person with old habits.

items.text: “You can't win them all.”

items.text: ___ gets what one pays for. (formal)

options: Teenagers say they can concentrate and still check social media.
Teenagers say one can concentrates and still check social media.

options: One need to learn how to initiate and engage in extended conversations.
Children need to learn how to initiate and engage in extended conversations.

options: When they don't have much human contact, they can become isolated.
When you doesn't have much human contact, they can become isolated.

talk.title: Social media: good or bad?
talk.task: Give Claude your opinion about social media for children and teens. Don't switch between they and you.
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Ask me to write 4-5 sentences about the advantages or disadvantages of social media for children and teenagers. Check one thing especially: I should use 'they / their' for people in general and not switch to impersonal 'you' in the middle (academic style). Show me any place where I switched.

items.title: another = one more
lines: One more of many. Singular.

examples.text: One subject that interests me is math. Another is psychology.

items.title: the other = the last one
lines: Only one is left.

examples.text: I'm taking two electives. One is sociology. The other is psychology.

items.text: Look at your hands. One is your right hand. ___ is your left hand.
items.why: Only two hands. The last one → The other.

items.title: others = some more
lines: Plural. Not all of the rest.

examples.text: Some movies are comedies. Others are dramas.

items.title: the others = all the rest
lines: Plural. Everything that is left.
chips: some … the others (nothing else is left)

examples.text: I found several movies. Some are comedies. The others are dramas.

items.title: With a noun: no s

examples.text: Other movies are dramas.
The other movies are dramas.
Others are dramas.
The others are dramas.

items.tip: ❌ others movies. An adjective never takes s.

items.text: Some people have red hair. ___ people have brown hair.
items.why: Before a noun (people) → Other, no s.

items.title: another + number
lines: another = more, even with a plural.
another = one more. the other = the last one.
others = some more. the others = all the rest. Before a noun: other (no s).

examples.text: One is sociology. The other is psychology.
Some are comedies. Others are dramas.
I need another five dollars.

items.text: You have five fingers. One is your thumb. ___ is your index finger.
___ is your middle finger.
___ finger is your ring finger.
And ___ finger (the last of the five) is your little finger.
Look at your hands. One is your right hand. ___ is your left hand.
items.why: Only two. The last one → The other.

items.text: I have two cell phone chargers. I keep one in the car and ___ next to my bed.
items.why: Two chargers. The last one → the other.

items.text: I'd like to buy ___ one and leave it in the kitchen.

items.why: One more / a different one → another.

items.why: Some more people (not all). Alone → Others.

items.text: Some people have red hair. ___ people have brown hair.
I have four children. One of them has red hair. ___ children have brown hair.
items.why: All the rest + noun → The other children.

items.text: I have four children. One of them has red hair. ___ have brown hair.
items.why: All the rest, alone → The others.

I'm almost finished. I just need ___ five minutes.

items.why: All the rest (two cities) → the others.

options: I need one more hour, maybe more.

talk.title: One… another… the other

One is ... / Some TV programs are excellent, but ... I complete it using another, the other, others or the others. Check that I choose the right form.

items.title: each other = both ways

items.title: one after the other
lines: One, then the next, then the next.
chips: The ducklings slipped into the water one after the other.

items.title: other than = except
lines: After a negative.
chips: No one knows my secret other than Rosa.
No one knows my secret except Rosa.

items.title: in other words
lines: Say it again, more simply.
chips: Fruit and vegetables are full of vitamins. In other words, they are good for you.

items.text: I'd prefer that you don't tell anyone. ___, I would like to keep this secret.
items.why: The expression is In other words.

lines: each other / one another = both ways. every other = skip one.
the other day = recently. other than = except. in other words = more simply.

examples.text: Mike and I write to each other every week.
I saw him just the other day.
No one knows my secret other than Rosa.

items.text: Lisa and Kate talk to each other every other day. → Kate talks to Lisa often.
They talk every other day. → Kate talked to Lisa today. She'll talk to her again tomorrow.
Kate saw Lisa the other day at the park. → Kate last saw Lisa a few weeks ago.
items.why: the other day = a few days ago.

items.text: Lisa's children were walking behind her, one after the other. → They were walking in a line.
items.why: one after the other = in a line.

items.text: Please write on every other line.
No one knows my secret other than Rosa.
Mike and I write to each other every week.
options: I write to him and he writes to me.
We both write to other people.

items.text: Fruit and vegetables are full of vitamins. ___, they are good for you.
items.why: in other words = to say it more simply.

items.text: Two countries border on the United States. One is Canada. ___ is Mexico.
items.why: Only two. The last one → The other.

items.text: One of the countries I would like to visit is Sweden. ___ is Malaysia.
Besides these two, there are many ___ places I would like to see.
Louis and I have been friends for a long time. We've known ___ since we were children.
I talked to Sam ___ day. — Oh? How is he?
items.why: the other day = a few days ago.

items.text: This area has no trees and very few plants ___ cactuses.
It has little or no rainfall. ___, this area is a desert.
items.why: Saying it more simply → In other words.

items.text: I'd like to go to the party, but I've already made ___ plans.
Some people are tall; ___ are short.
Some people are nearsighted; ___ people are farsighted.
Mr. and Mrs. Jay love ___. They are a happily married couple.
How often do you travel to Portland? — Every ___ month I go there.
I have nothing to write with ___ this pencil.
My niece ate one cookie after ___ until she finished the whole box.
The baby ducks walked in a line behind their mother, one after ___.
They support each other. ___, they are a happy couple.
items.why: The expression is In other words.

items.say: I spend a lot of time with my grandmother. We enjoy each other's company.
options: My grandmother and I like to spend time with others.
I enjoy spending time with my grandmother.

items.say: Other than Maria, all of the students had the wrong answer.
options: All of the students had the wrong answer.
Some students had the wrong answer, but Maria didn't.

items.say: The Clarks see each other only on weekends.
options: The Clarks each see other people on weekends.
The Clarks spend time together on weekends.

items.say: Susan spoke with him just the other day.
options: Susan spoke with him a long time ago.

items.say: No one other than Tom, Anna and me knows about the engagement.
options: Three people know about the engagement.
Four people know about the engagement.

items.say: Everyone other than Jan knows about the party.
options: Jan doesn't know about the party.

talk.title: Some… others…
talk.task: Finish Claude's sentences with a form of other: “Some people like coffee while others prefer tea.”
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English speaking partner. Give me one pattern at a time to complete with my own ideas: I have two ___. One is ___, and (other) ___ is ___. / Some people like to ___ in their free time. (Other) ___ prefer ___. / There are three ___ that I especially like. One is ___. (Other) ___ is ___. (Other) ___ is ___. Check my use of another, the other, others, the others, each other.

talk.title: Texting in meetings
talk.task: Is checking messages in class or in a meeting OK? Give three reasons: First… Another reason… Finally…
talk.claudePrompt: You are my English writing partner. Ask me to choose one question (Is checking text messages in class appropriate? / What are three advantages of the Internet? / What is your opinion of selfies?) and write one paragraph with three reasons, using 'First, ...', 'Another reason/problem is ...', 'Finally, ...'. Check my pronouns (they/their consistency, object pronouns) and my use of another / other.

items.text: My friends and I ordered Indian food. I wasn't very hungry, but I ate most of [them].
options: My friends and I ordered Indian food. I wasn't very hungry, but I ate most of it.
My friends and I ordered Indian food. I wasn't very hungry, but I ate most of its.
My friends and me ordered Indian food. I wasn't very hungry, but I ate most of them.

items.text: My brother used to play tennis with my sister and [I] every day after school.
options: My brother used to play tennis with my sister and my every day after school.
My brother used to play tennis with my sister and me every day after school.
My brother used to play tennis with I and my sister every day after school.

items.text: My cousin and her husband moved to [other] city because they don't like cold weather.
options: My cousin and her husband moved to others city because they don't like cold weather.
My cousin and her husband moved to the others city because they don't like cold weather.
My cousin and her husband moved to another city because they don't like cold weather.

items.text: If you want to pass your exams, you need to study very hard for [it].
options: If you want to pass your exams, you need to study very hard for them.
If you want to pass your exams, you need to study very hard for its.
If you want to pass your exams, you need to study very hard for they.

items.text: I like to travel because I like to learn about other [country] and [custom].
options: I like to travel because I like to learn about another countries and customs.
I like to travel because I like to learn about other countries and customs.
I like to travel because I like to learn about others country and custom.

items.text: When I lost my passport, I had to apply for [other] one.
options: When I lost my passport, I had to apply for another one.
When I lost my passport, I had to apply for others one.
When I lost my passport, I had to apply for the others one.

items.text: When I got to class, all of the [others] students were already in [his] seats.
options: When I got to class, all of the others students were already in their seats.
When I got to class, all of the other students were already in his seats.
When I got to class, all of the other students were already in their seats.

items.text: In hot weather, you need to water the plants every other [days].
options: In hot weather, you need to water the plants every others day.
In hot weather, you need to water the plants every other day.
In hot weather, you need to water the plants every another day.

items.text: I live in a two-room apartment. [Its] too small for [mine] family.
options: I live in a two-room apartment. It's too small for my family.
I live in a two-room apartment. Its too small for my family.
I live in a two-room apartment. It's too small for mine family.
items.why: It is → It's. Before a noun → my.

items.text: A child needs to learn how to get along with [another] people and how to depend on [yourself].
options: A child needs to learn how to get along with others people and how to depend on himself.
A child needs to learn how to get along with other people and how to depend on himself or herself.
A child needs to learn how to get along with another people and how to depend on themselves.
items.why: other + plural noun. A child → himself or herself.

items.text: [Other from] Tom, everyone has responded to the wedding invitation.
options: Other than Tom, everyone has responded to the wedding invitation.
Another from Tom, everyone has responded to the wedding invitation.
Others than Tom, everyone has responded to the wedding invitation.

items.text: Mr. Gray asked to speak to Mona and [I]. He explained the policies and asked for [ours] opinions.
options: Mr. Gray asked to speak to Mona and I. He explained the policies and asked for our opinions.
Mr. Gray asked to speak to Mona and me. He explained the policies and asked for ours opinions.
Mr. Gray asked to speak to Mona and me. He explained the policies and asked for our opinions.

items.text: My cousins asked to borrow my car because [their's] was in the garage for repairs.
options: My cousins asked to borrow my car because their was in the garage for repairs.
My cousins asked to borrow my car because theirs was in the garage for repairs.
My cousins asked to borrow my car because they's was in the garage for repairs.
items.why: Possessive pronouns have no apostrophe: theirs.

items.text: The players were looking at one [anothers], trying to find their weakest opponent.
options: The players were looking at one another, trying to find their weakest opponent.
The players were looking at one others, trying to find their weakest opponent.
The players were looking at ones another, trying to find their weakest opponent.

items.text: The manager introduced Manuel and [I] to the other employees in the new branch office.
options: The manager introduced Manuel and my to the other employees in the new branch office.
The manager introduced I and Manuel to the other employees in the new branch office.
The manager introduced Manuel and me to the other employees in the new branch office.

items.text: A hippopotamus spends most of [it's] time in the water of rivers and lakes.
options: A hippopotamus spends most of it time in the water of rivers and lakes.
A hippopotamus spends most of its time in the water of rivers and lakes.
A hippopotamus spends most of its' time in the water of rivers and lakes.
items.why: Belonging to it → its. No apostrophe.
